message.reasoning:
We need to generate high-quality unit test code for BaseJsonValidator.collectAnnotations(ExecutionContext) covering many cases described in JSON test cases.

We have a test class framework already. It defines TestValidator subclass with overridden collectAnnotations(ExecutionContext, String) returning preset returnValue. However many test cases require behavior based on ExecutionContext flags, keyword null/empty, etc. We may need to extend TestValidator to allow custom getKeyword behavior (including null, empty, exception). Also need to mock ExecutionContext behavior: methods like isCollectAnnotationsEnabled()? We need to inspect ExecutionContext class but not given. We can assume it has method isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() returning boolean. Also maybe getAnnotations() etc.

But we can use Mockito to mock ExecutionContext and stub methods accordingly.

The BaseJsonValidator.collectAnnotations(ExecutionContext) method's internal logic is not shown, but we can infer: It likely checks if executionContext is null -> return false; else if executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() is false -> return false; else if keyword is null or empty -> return false; else call collectAnnotations(executionContext, keyword) and return its result.

Thus we need to test these scenarios.

Implementation: We'll create a subclass of BaseJsonValidator (TestValidator) that allows us to set returnValue for the overloaded method, and also override getKeyword to return a configurable value (maybe via constructor). Also we may need to have a subclass that throws exception in getKeyword.

We'll use reflection to invoke the protected collectAnnotations(ExecutionContext) method if needed, but we already have invokeCollectAnnotations method.

Test cases:

Group: basic delegation – already covered.

But we need to implement more tests per JSON.

We'll create parameterized tests using @ParameterizedTest and @MethodSource to supply ExecutionContext mocks and expected outcomes.

But for clarity, we can write separate test methods for each scenario.

Let's design:

- Test when executionContext is null -> expect false (no delegation). Use validator with returnValue true but should return false because null.

- Test when executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() returns false -> expect false.

- Test when executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() returns true but keyword is null -> expect false. We'll create subclass that overrides getKeyword to return null.

- Test when keyword empty string -> expect false.

- Test when keyword non-null and enabled -> delegate and return true/false based on overridden method.

- Test when overloaded method throws RuntimeException -> wrapper propagates.

- Test when getKeyword throws RuntimeException -> propagate.

- Test when executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() throws IllegalStateException / NullPointerException / IllegalArgumentException -> propagate.

- Test when overloaded method throws AssertionError (Error) -> propagate.

We'll need to mock ExecutionContext's isCollectAnnotationsEnabled method; also maybe getAnnotations? Not needed.

We'll need to create a subclass that can be configured with returnValue and maybe exception throwing in overloaded method.

Define TestValidator with fields:

- Boolean returnValue (or maybe Supplier<Boolean> to allow exception). Simpler: we can subclass for exception case.

We'll create inner classes:

- TestValidator (normal) – as before.

- ExceptionThrowingValidator extends TestValidator overrides collectAnnotations to throw exception.

- KeywordExceptionValidator extends TestValidator overrides getKeyword to throw.

- NullKeywordValidator extends TestValidator overrides getKeyword to return null.

- EmptyKeywordValidator returns "".

We'll also need to create a constructor that accepts keyword string.

Simplify: Base TestValidator with fields returnValue, keyword (String), and maybe a flag to throw in collectAnnotations.

Implementation:

class TestValidator extends BaseJsonValidator {
    private final Boolean returnValue;
    private final String keyword;
    private final RuntimeException overloadException;
    private final RuntimeException keywordException;

    Constructor takes returnValue, keyword, overloadException, keywordException.

    getKeyword returns keyword unless keywordException != null then throw.

    collectAnnotations(ExecutionContext, String) either throws overloadException if not null else returns returnValue.

}

Thus we can configure each scenario.

Now write test methods.

We'll need to import mocks: ExecutionContext.

Assume ExecutionContext class has method isCollectAnnotationsEnabled() returning boolean. We'll mock with Mockito.

Also maybe method getAnnotations() but not needed.

Now implement tests.

Test 1: null executionContext -> expect false.

Test 2: executionContext enabled false -> false.

Test 3: executionContext enabled true, keyword null -> false.

Test 4: keyword empty -> false.

Test 5: enabled true, keyword non-null, overload returns true -> true.

Test 6: overload returns false -> false.

Test 7: overload throws RuntimeException -> expect RuntimeException.

Test 8: getKeyword throws RuntimeException -> expect RuntimeException.

Test 9: executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled throws IllegalStateException -> expect IllegalStateException.

Test 10: executionContext.isCollectAnnotationsEnabled throws NullPointerException -> expect NullPointerException.

Test 11: overload throws AssertionError -> expect AssertionError.

We can combine some using @ParameterizedTest.

But for clarity, separate methods.

Now code.

Need to add @Mock ExecutionContext executionContext; but we need multiple mocks with different behavior per test; we can create them inside test methods using Mockito.mock.

Add imports: org.mockito.Mockito, org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest, org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource, java.util.stream.Stream, org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments, static org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments.arguments;

But may not need parameterized.

We'll keep simple.

Now produce final test class code.

Note: BaseJsonValidator constructor signature: we saw super(schemaLocation, evaluationPath, schemaNode, parentSchema, validatorType, validationContext); So we need to call super with those mocks. Already done.

Now implement TestValidator with fields.

Implementation details: Since BaseJsonValidator is abstract and implements JsonValidator, we must implement abstract methods: getKeyword (already), collectAnnotations overloaded, maybe getEvaluationPath? Actually BaseJsonValidator implements JsonValidator which may have many abstract methods; but we only need to implement those required for compilation. In the earlier framework they only overrode getKeyword and collectAnnotations overload. However BaseJsonValidator also has abstract methods like getEvaluationPath? Let's check: In class definition, getEvaluationPath() is overridden (maybe from JsonValidator). It likely has default implementation in BaseJsonValidator? Actually BaseJsonValidator implements JsonValidator, and provides getEvaluationPath() method (annotated @Override) but not abstract. So maybe only abstract methods are getKeyword() (abstract), maybe getNodeFieldType? Not sure. But earlier test compiled with just overriding getKeyword and collectAnnotations overload. So we can keep same.

Thus our TestValidator extends BaseJsonValidator and overrides getKeyword and collectAnnotations overload.

We'll add fields for keyword and overloadException.

Implementation:

private final String keyword;
private final RuntimeException overloadException;
private final Boolean returnValue;

Constructor:

TestValidator(Boolean returnValue, String keyword, RuntimeException overloadException, RuntimeException keywordException, ... ) { super(...); this.returnValue = returnValue; this.keyword = keyword; this.overloadException = overloadException; this.keywordException = keywordException; }

getKeyword:

if (keywordException != null) throw keywordException;
return keyword;

collectAnnotations overload:

if (overloadException != null) throw overloadException;
return returnValue != null ? returnValue : false;

Now tests.

Now code.
